paras: The threatened lynching of Henry Washington and Cora Bolen took place in Sharon, Pennsylvania, in early June 1903, when a crowd made threats of lynching against the two Black prisoners, who had been jailed over the death of Washington's six-year-old son. The crowd "lacked a leader" and no attack followed; both prisoners were tried later that month, convicted and sentenced.

Washington and his sister-in-law, Cora Bolen, described as "both negroes," were committed to jail without bail for causing the death of Willie Washington, aged six. The father said that his other son, James, aged seven, had thrown a shoe at Willie and caused fatal injuries. James denied this and said Bolen had beaten Willie over the head with a poker, burned both boys with hot irons and once set Willie on a red-hot stove; his own leg was in bandages.

According to the wire report, "Threats of lynching were freely made, but the crowd lacked a leader." The Wheeling Register's version placed the threats "last night" and the commitment "to-day" under a June 7 dateline, although the same text had appeared in Washington on June 5 with the commitment dated "yesterday." No report describes any move against the jail.

Washington and Bolen were tried before a jury at Mercer, which deliberated three hours before returning a guilty verdict, reported as voluntary manslaughter. James testified that his father and Bolen had chained the two boys to the floor and beaten them with clubs, and the boys' stepmother corroborated him. Judge Miller sentenced Washington to ten years on the first count and one year on the second, and he was taken to the Western penitentiary; Bolen was sent to reform school. The trial reports gave Bolen's age as thirteen, not sixteen as at her arrest.

The case reached readers only through white papers carrying wire copy, from the Washington Times on June 5 to the Spokane Press on July 9. The first story ran as "GIRL BRANDS BOY WITH HOT IRONS, HE SAYS" and mentioned the lynching threats only in its last sentence, without comment. Verdict stories under headlines such as "GUILTY OF ROASTING LITTLE BOY TO DEATH" and "Fiendish Father Kills Son By Abuse" dwelt on the torture and did not mention the threats. No Black-press coverage of the case was found.

bases: The only racial violence reported is a crowd that 'freely made' threats of lynching against two jailed Black prisoners accused of causing a child's death; no attack followed (A1, A2).
No one was killed or attacked: the crowd that threatened to lynch Washington and Bolen 'lacked a leader', and both were later tried, convicted and sentenced by a court (A1, A3, A4).
The lynching threats rest on one wire story printed twice (A1, A2); the later trial reports (A3, A4, A5) confirm the prosecution but do not mention the threats.

framing.detail: The first report, headlined 'GIRL BRANDS BOY WITH HOT IRONS, HE SAYS', identified the accused as 'negroes' and mentioned the lynching threats in one closing sentence without comment.

Trial reports ran under 'GUILTY OF ROASTING LITTLE BOY TO DEATH', 'ROASTED HIS SON / Fiendish Father Kills Son By Abuse' and 'FATHER TORTURED A SMALL SON TO DEATH', centering the torture and dropping the lynching threat.
